messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Prosecutor
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 33

She is 44, married, and has spent much of her adult life in courtrooms, speaking with measured precision as a prosecutor. Before the war, she describes herself as someone who trusted order: laws, schedules, documents stacked neatly in folders, doors locked at night. She had built a life around the belief that chaos could be contained if one stayed prepared. When the fighting reaches her city, that belief begins to unravel.

At first, the danger feels distant and almost abstract. She hears shelling from farther districts and follows the news with the same disciplined attention she once gave case files. Then the sounds move closer. Windows rattle. Power cuts become routine. She continues working as long as she can, helping with cases when the courts still function, but each trip to the office feels narrower, more perilous. She starts carrying her documents in a way that allows her to leave quickly. She notices how her body stays tense, even while she tells herself to remain calm.

The event that changes everything happens on an ordinary errand. She is in the street when a strike lands nearby. The blast is not only loud; it is physically disorienting, a force that seems to enter her chest and stop time. She remembers the sudden white flash, people dropping to the ground, the raw instinct to run without knowing where. She thinks she is dying for a few seconds, and later she cannot fully explain why that certainty felt so absolute. Dust fills the air. She cannot hear properly at first. Her hands shake so badly that she has trouble finding her phone. She sees injured people and moving bodies and has a brief, terrifying sense that the world has become unrecognizable.

Afterward, she does what many around her do: she keeps moving. She returns home, checks on family, and tries to sound steady. But the experience settles into her body in ways that make daily life feel altered. Sleep becomes fragmented. The first weeks are filled with waking at every noise, her heart pounding before she is fully conscious. She begins to scan streets automatically, looking for open spaces, damaged buildings, routes of escape. In court, she catches herself sitting closest to the door. She is still capable, still precise, still the person others rely on, but she works with a new strain, as if part of her attention never leaves the possibility of danger.

Over time, she starts avoiding anything that reminds her of the blast. She stops going near the place where it happened. She changes routes, leaves conversations when people talk too casually about the war, and turns away from news footage if it shows rubble or ambulances. She says she is simply trying not to dwell on things, but there is a clear effort in it, a constant management of what she can bear. Sometimes an unexpected bang—a slammed car door, fireworks, a heavy book dropped in the office—sends a jolt through her body before her mind can catch up. Her chest tightens, and for a moment she is back on that street, with the same immediate certainty of threat.

She also notices that she has become more irritable and less patient, especially at home. Small frustrations feel oversized. She is ashamed of how quickly she snaps with her husband, who is trying in his own way to keep life stable. She loves him, but she feels separated from him by something she cannot fully name. At times she sits beside him and feels oddly distant, as if she is watching her life from a slight remove. Her memory feels less reliable than it once did. She loses track of details, rereads the same page, and worries that she is no longer as sharp as she needs to be in a profession built on credibility and control.

Months later, the war is still present in the background of every decision, but her life has narrowed around endurance. She continues to work when possible, because work gives shape to the day and because her identity is deeply tied to being useful, orderly, and composed. Yet she arrives tired, sleeps lightly, and carries a constant readiness in her muscles. She describes herself as functioning, but only by exerting great effort. There are moments when she is sitting in her office, listening to a colleague speak, and suddenly realizes she has been holding her breath. Other times, she catches herself imagining the sound of a blast before it happens and feels her body brace in advance, as if it has learned that peace is temporary.
